etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 雨 ‘rain’ + phonetic 令; the oracle-bone form shows raindrops falling. Its meanings include ‘light rain’, ‘fragmentary, remainder’ and ‘zero’.

funFacts: Years are read digit by digit and the zero is written 〇: 二〇二六年 èr líng èr liù nián ‘(the year) 2026’.
pitfalls: Inside a number, 零 is said once for any run of empty places: 1005 = 一千零五 yìqiān líng wǔ, not *一千零零五.
subtleties: 101 is 一百零一, but 110 is 一百一十 — 零 only marks an empty place in the middle.

etymology.text: Ideogram: two parallel strokes, as 一 is one stroke and 三 three. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kV-ni-s, cognate with Tibetan gnyis.

funFacts: 二百五 ‘two hundred and fifty’ is slang for ‘a fool, an idiot’ — avoid that number in jokes about people.
pitfalls: Before a measure word say 两: 两个学生, not *二个学生. Inside numbers it is always 二: 十二个, 二十二个.
Ordinals and digits keep 二: 第二 ‘second’, 二号 ‘number two’.
subtleties: For 200 and 2000 both 二百 / 两百 and 二千 / 两千 are heard; 两千 is the usual everyday form.

etymology.text: Shuowen Jiezi explains 兩 as 一 + 㒳 (a pair); Baxter sees two 丙 side by side. The origin of the word is unknown (Schuessler proposes a Kra-Dai loan).

funFacts: Restaurants in the north still sell dumplings by the 两 (tael, 50 g): 二两饺子 — here 二 comes before the unit 两.
pitfalls: 两 replaces 二 only directly before a measure word or a unit: 两个, 两本, 两岁 — but 十二个, 二十二个, 第二个.
Spoken liǎng: like every 3rd tone, it changes to 2nd before another 3rd tone (两本 liáng běn), though it is still written liǎng.
subtleties: 两 and 二 are the same number: 二 is the name of the digit, 两 the amount ‘two of something’ — like English ‘two’ vs ‘a pair / both’.
In a large number the first 2 may be 两: 两百 / 二百 ‘200’, 两千 ‘2000’, 两万 ‘20 000’ — both are correct, 两 is more colloquial.

pitfalls: On cheques the forgery-proof form 叁 is written instead.

etymology.text: Originally a pictogram of breath coming out of the nose, borrowed for the sound of ‘four’; earlier ‘four’ was written with four strokes (亖). From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *pV-lij.

funFacts: Because 四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ ‘to die’, many buildings in China have no 4th floor, and phone numbers full of 4s are cheap.
pitfalls: 四 sì (4th tone) and 十 shí (2nd tone) are easy to confuse in fast speech, especially 四十 sìshí ‘40’ and 十四 shísì ‘14’ — listen for the order of the tones.
subtleties: The tongue-twister 四是四，十是十，十四是十四，四十是四十 trains exactly this difference.

etymology.text: Originally written with an X between two bars; its first meaning is disputed (a tally mark, ‘to cross’, …). From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *l-ŋaʔ ‘five’.

funFacts: Five ‘elements’ (五行: wood, fire, earth, metal, water) organise traditional Chinese medicine and cosmology.
pitfalls: 五 wǔ is a 3rd tone: in 五百 ‘500’ it is said wú bǎi (3rd-tone change), though written wǔ.
subtleties: The China flag has five stars: 五星红旗 ‘the five-star red flag’.

subtleties: Chinese count 6–10 on one hand with special signs: 六 is thumb + little finger, 八 thumb + index finger, 十 crossed index fingers or a fist.

subtleties: Ordinals and dates are regular: 第七 ‘seventh’, 七月七日 ‘the 7th of July’ (the Qixi date of the lunar calendar is the 7th day of the 7th month).

etymology.text: In the oracle bones a single vertical stroke; the cross shape came later. Origin discussed (perhaps the original form of 针 ‘needle’).

pitfalls: 10 is just 十, never *一十 — but inside a bigger number the 一 comes back: 110 = 一百一十.
subtleties: 十 builds the numbers 11–99: 十 + digit for 11–19 (十五), digit + 十 for the tens (五十), digit + 十 + digit for the rest (五十五).

etymology.text: 一 ‘one’ + 百 ‘hundred’ (phono-semantic: 一 + phonetic 白; from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *pV-rja(k)).

funFacts: Chinese exams are often marked out of 100, so 一百分 is the dream mark — and 百分之百 ‘a hundred out of a hundred’ means ‘one hundred per cent’.
pitfalls: Say 一百, not just *百: the 一 is needed (unlike 十 for 10). Spoken yìbǎi — 一 changes to 4th tone before 3rd-tone 百.
subtleties: 百 alone also means ‘all, many’ in set words: 百货 ‘all kinds of goods’ (a department store is 百货商店).

etymology.text: 一 ‘one’ + 千 ‘thousand’ (一 + phonetic 人 — the two words sounded alike in Old Chinese).

funFacts: The Arabian Nights are 《一千零一夜》 ‘one thousand and one nights’ in Chinese — the same number as Arabic ألف ليلة وليلة.
pitfalls: Chinese counts large numbers in groups of four digits: 10 000 is 一万, not *十千; 100 000 is 十万.
subtleties: 千 also means ‘very many’: 千万 ‘by all means’ (literally ‘thousands and tens of thousands’).

etymology.text: 很 ‘very’ + 多 ‘many’.

funFacts: 好多 ‘good-many’ is the colloquial twin of 很多 — compare English ‘a good many’.
pitfalls: 多 alone hardly ever stands before a noun: say 很多书, not *多书.
As the predicate the amount comes last: 人很多 ‘there are many people’ — not *很多是人.
subtleties: 很 in 很多 is not felt as ‘very’: 很多 is the plain ‘many’; for ‘very many’ say 非常多.

etymology.text: Ideogrammic compound: two pieces of meat (肉), later written as two 夕. One explanation: in ancient times two pieces of meat was a lot.

funFacts: 多少 ‘many-few’ is the question ‘how many, how much?’ — Chinese often makes abstract words from opposites, like 大小 ‘size’ (big-small).
pitfalls: 多 alone hardly ever stands before a noun in everyday speech: 很多人, not *多人.
After a number 多 means ‘over’: 二十多岁 ‘in one’s twenties’ — and it stands before the measure word: 三十多个, 一千多本.
subtleties: Like all Chinese adjectives 多 is a predicate on its own, no 是: 人多 ‘there are many people’; a bare 多 sounds like a contrast (这里人多，那里人少).

etymology.text: Pictogram: small dots, perhaps grains of sand, for ‘a few, a little’; related to 小 ‘small’, which has three dots.

funFacts: 多少 ‘many-few’ means ‘how many?’ — the opposites 多 and 少 together ask for the amount.
pitfalls: 少 does not stand before a noun on its own: not *少人, *少书. Use it as the predicate (人很少 ‘there are few people’) or say 很少有人 … ‘few people …’.
Read shào it is another word, ‘young’: 少年 ‘teenager’, 少女 ‘young girl’.
subtleties: 很少 before a verb means ‘seldom’: 我很少喝咖啡 ‘I seldom drink coffee’.

etymology.text: 不 ‘not’ + 多 ‘many’.

funFacts: The writer Hu Shi mocked the habit of ‘near enough’ in his satirical essay 差不多先生传 ‘Mr. Close-Enough’ — 差不多 ‘differs not much’.
pitfalls: 不多 normally stands after the thing it describes, as the predicate: 人不多 ‘there aren’t many people’, not *不多人.
Do not confuse it with 不少 ‘quite a lot’: 朋友不多 ‘not many friends’, 朋友不少 ‘quite a few friends’.
subtleties: 不多 is the softer, more modest way to say ‘few’: 我朋友不多 sounds less sad than 我朋友很少.

etymology.text: 一 ‘one’ + 点 ‘dot, drop’ (traditional 點, 黑 ‘black’ + phonetic 占): ‘one dot’ of something.

funFacts: In the north people say yìdiǎnr and write 一点儿; Taiwan and the south say and write 一点 (一點).
pitfalls: 一点 comes AFTER an adjective (贵一点 ‘a bit more expensive’), 有点 BEFORE it (有点贵 ‘a bit too expensive’).
Spoken yìdiǎn: 一 takes the 4th tone before the 3rd-tone 点.
subtleties: 一点 makes a request softer: 快一点 ‘a bit faster’, 多吃一点 ‘eat a bit more’.

subtleties: 所有 + noun may take 的 or not: 所有学生 / 所有的学生 — both are correct.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 者 + semantic 邑 ‘town’ (the reading dū ‘capital’). The adverb ‘all’ is a colloquial form of 諸 ‘all’ (Schuessler).

funFacts: Read dū the same character means ‘capital’: 首都 ‘capital city’, and it is in the city name 成都 Chéngdū.
pitfalls: 都 stands before the verb, never before the subject: 我们都是学生, not *都我们是学生.
都 sums up what comes BEFORE it: in 他们都有书 it is ‘they all’, not ‘all the books’.
subtleties: With two people 都 means ‘both’: 我和他都是老师 ‘He and I are both teachers.’
都不 is ‘none of …’, 不都 ‘not all’: 他们都不是老师 vs 他们不都是老师.

override.pos: Wiktionary files 一些 as a noun and an adverb; it is the numeral 一 + the measure word 些 and stands before a noun like a determiner (一些书 ‘some books’), so it is filed here as DET.

profile.feeling: Some, a few — an amount you do not count exactly.

senses.def: some, a few, a little (an indefinite amount)
(after an adjective) a bit, slightly: 好一些 ‘a bit better’

examples.text: 一些书在这里，一些书在那里。
examples.py: Yìxiē shū zài zhèli, yìxiē shū zài nàli.
examples.tr: Some books are here, some are over there.

synonyms.nuance: ‘some (of them)’, as opposed to others — usually at the start: 有些人…
‘a little’ — a small amount, mostly of things not counted

etymology.text: 一 ‘one’ + 些, the measure word for an indefinite amount (as in 这些, 那些).

funFacts: 些 is the measure word of ‘more than one, not counted’: 这些 ‘these’, 那些 ‘those’, 一些 ‘some’.
pitfalls: 一些 takes no other measure word: 一些书, not *一些本书.
Spoken yìxiē: 一 takes the 4th tone before 1st-tone 些.
subtleties: 一些 can be a few or quite a lot; 一点 is always small: 一些朋友, but 一点水.

‘some’ — also after the verb (我买了一些书)

etymology.text: 有 ‘there are’ + 些 ‘some, a few’: ‘there are some (who) …’.

funFacts: 有些人 is literally ‘there are some people (who)’ — that is why it likes to stand at the start of a sentence.
pitfalls: 有些 + noun belongs at the start of the sentence; after a verb say 一些: 我买了一些书, not *我买了有些书.
subtleties: 有些 contrasts a part with the rest: 有些人喜欢，有些人不喜欢 ‘some like it, some don’t’.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 彳 + phonetic 艮. First meaning ‘to disobey; cruel’ (like 狠); used for ‘very’ since the Yuan dynasty.

funFacts: 很 once meant ‘fierce, cruel’ — the same sound written 狠 hěn still does.
pitfalls: A Chinese adjective needs a link, but not 是: 他很高 ‘he is tall’, not *他是高. A bare adjective sounds like a comparison: 这里人多，那里人少.
subtleties: In 很好 and 很多 the 很 is usually not heard as ‘very’; stress it to mean ‘very’.
